title: Resume cutover playbook + TF compatibility notes for private deploys
body:
Purpose and scope:
This is a pragmatic, prescriptive runbook for 'resuming a cutover' after a failed or partially-applied upgrade for Private Deployments (VPC / on-prem). Focus: get customer workloads back online within agreed RTO while preserving data integrity (RPO targets) and minimizing manual state surgery. This doc combines DR steps, Terraform compatibility notes and quick workarounds for common state/blocker patterns we see in the field.

When to use this doc:
- Upgrade or migration started and failure occurred mid-cutover (some infra updated, some not).
- Restores required after partial restore/rollback attempt.
- Customer-facing incident where we must resume and finish a controlled cutover with minimal downtime.

High-level resumable cutover strategy (phases and time budgets):
- Phase 0: Triage & pause (0-30m): stop automated jobs, notify stakeholders, take orchestration snapshot (see comms).
- Phase 1: Confirm state & RPO (30-90m): decide whether to continue from current infra state or perform fresh restore from snapshot.
- Phase 2: Minimal service restore (RTO target window) (90m-4h): bring control plane and critical services up (auth, config, router, storage).
- Phase 3: Data finalization & model artifact sync (4h-12h): rehydrate caches, import model shards, run smoke/e2e tests.
- Phase 4: Cutover finish & verification (12h+): finalize DNS/route cut, thumbs-up from customer, postmortem scheduling.

Key principles:
- Prefer immutable snapshots (S3, object storage, or block snapshot) over manual per-resource recovery.
- If Terraform state drift is present, prefer import + plan over editing statefiles directly. Only edit state as last resort with approvals.
- Maintain encryption key continuity: if KMS keys were rotated mid-cutover, rehydrate older key access first (see KMS section).
- Preflight automated verification steps before permitting traffic cut.

Immediate triage checklist (first 30 minutes):
- Who: Incident lead (on-call SRE) + Private Deploy eng owner + Customer success rep.
- Actions:
  - Mark maintenance window in customer console and Slack channel.
  - Freeze CI/CD jobs that target the cluster.
  - Snapshot current cluster state: etcd snapshot (if applicable), DB logical backup, filesystem snapshot ID, object storage version ID. Record checksums (sha256).
  - Identify which terraform modules applied successfully (check terraform apply logs, CI run ids, terraform state list).
  - Record last known working commit and PR for control plane and infra modules.

Decision fork: Continue vs Full Restore
- Continue (less disruption): if only non-critical modules failed or reconcilable drift exists (e.g., missing lb rules). Also when latest snapshot age <= RPO.
- Full restore: if partial database migrations ran and cannot be cleanly rolled back, or object storage commit mismatch, or snapshot integrity questionable.

Terraform compatibility and state surgery notes (common issues & fixes):
- Backend and lock: always verify remote backend availability (S3 + DDB lock or Consul). If lock stuck: use terraform force-unlock after confirming operator ownership.
  - Example: terraform force-unlock -force 12345678-90ab-cdef-1234-567890abcdef
- Provider version skew: known breaking bump: aws provider v4.x -> v5.x sometimes changes resource schema. If PR upgraded provider mid-cutover, pin previous provider in CLI to run plan:
  - export TF_PROVIDER_OVERRIDE=registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws@~>4.60
- Partial resource creation: use terraform import to bring resources into state rather than re-create. Import pattern:
  - terraform import module.nlb.aws_lb.nlb arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:us-west-2:123456789012:loadbalancer/net/my-nlb/abcd1234
- State drift with schema mismatch: if state has unexpected attributes, run terraform state replace-provider to map old provider namespace to new provider before plan.
- Manual state edit: last resort. Always check SHA256 and create backup of statefile before edit. Use the CLI helper: tfstate-guard.sh to snapshot and push to secure bucket.

Database restoration patterns (Postgres primary examples):
- Preferred: point-in-time recovery (PITR) using basebackup + WAL archive.
  - Steps:
    1) restore base backup to target host (chronological order),
    2) restore WAL segments from object storage until desired recovery_time,
    3) start in recovery mode, monitor logs for replay completion,
    4) promote to primary and run schema check scripts.
- If partial migration applied pre-cutover: do not promote; instead restore to earlier recovery_time pre-migration, then re-run migrations under controlled CI job.
- Example commands (psql / pg_basebackup):
  - pg_basebackup -h backup-host -D /var/lib/postgresql/data -R -X fetch -P
  - restore_command = 'aws s3 cp s3://private-deploy-wal/%f %p'

Object storage & model artifacts:
- Large model shards should be restored from incremental object snapshots. For huge models (>1TB) prefer rsync-style transfer between on-prem object stores.
- Maintain manifest file with sha256 per shard. After restore, run parallel checksum verification (GNU parallel).
- If artifacts are compressed/encrypted, ensure KMS/HSM access is available and test a single shard decrypt before bulk restore.

KV cache / runtime cache rehydration:
- We do not rely on caches for durability. Plan for cold-cache behavior after restore.
- To speed up recovery for high-traffic endpoints: re-warm hot prefixes using recorded request logs + replay harness (see linked artifact helper).
- For stateful KV stores (etcd/consul): use native snapshot restore commands and ensure cluster ID and peer URLs are consistent.

KMS/HSM and key rotation notes:
- If key rotation happened mid-cutover, restore procedure must ensure old key material is importable or allow a temporary key alias pointing to prior key. Work with customer KMS admin for short window.
- Avoid re-encrypting blobs until service stable; keep original ciphertext and re-wrap in background.

Network/CNI and DNS considerations (VPC & on-prem):
- Ensure subnets and route tables were not half-applied. Confirm BGP peerings or transit gateways status.
- Validate DNS TTLs: if cutover reverts/advances, set low TTL pre-drill (30-60s) for faster rollback.
- Load balancers: avoid reusing DNS names until health checks pass across all AZs; use temporary hostname for canary traffic.

Sticky notes: immediate commands to check status
- terraform workspace show
- terraform state list | sed -n '1,80p'
- aws s3api head-object --bucket private-deploy-backups --key snapshots/2024-09-18/manifest.json
- consul operator raft list-peers (if using consul for state)

Resume-cutover workflow (detailed step-by-step):
1) Freeze: lockout automated deployments, alert customer and internal channels.
2) Snapshot: capture current etcd, db, object storage snapshot IDs and checksums.
3) Validate snapshots: small-file checksum, try a test restore to ephemeral host (not production).
4) Decide: continue vs full restore per decision fork above.

If continuing (recommended when safe):
- Reconcile terraform state: import missing resources, pin providers to pre-cutover versions and re-run terraform plan.
- Re-run infra modules that were interrupted (LBs, target groups, node pools) with parallelization limited to 2-3 modules at a time.
- Reconcile database migrations: if migration partially ran, use migration tool to mark unexecuted steps or rerun under maintenance flag.
- Reattach object storage buckets and verify manifest checksums.
- Start control plane services with low traffic, enable read-only mode for customer apps if available, run smoke tests.

If doing full restore:
- Create fresh cluster/environment with clean terraform apply using known-good commit and provider pins.
- Restore DB via PITR to target recovery_time.
- Restore object storage from snapshot manifest, validate checksums.
- Import necessary infra resources into terraform state for the new cluster (route tables, static IPs).
- Swap routes/DNS in maintenance window to minimize split-brain.

Smoke tests and verification (must pass before traffic cut):
- Control plane health: /health endpoints for frontend, scheduler, and model-worker return 200.
- Runtime correctness: sample prompts (3 per critical route) produce consistent embeddings or low-level errors. Record token latency must be within baseline +/-25%.
- Data integrity: row counts for production-critical tables must match snapshot manifest allowances.
- External integrations: KMS decrypt test, object storage read/write test, telemetry export to internal observability.

Rollback triggers and safeguards:
- >=10% degradation in tail latency for 5 consecutive minutes.
- Persistent 5xx rate >1% for 3 minutes on critical routes.
- Data re-sync failure (checksums mismatch after 3 tries).
- If any rollback trigger fires, revert DNS/route and open immediate postmortem ticket.

Post-recovery tasks:
- Run full data consistency checks overnight.
- Create postmortem, include timeline and exact terraform logs + commands used.
- Schedule a CR for terraform module changes that caused the issue.
- Re-run/update preflight CI that validates partial-apply behavior (add test case for the specific failure).

Terraform module notes & recommended quick patches:
- For modules that update LB / IP allocations: add a precondition guard variable (allow_partial_apply = false) to avoid half-applies in future.
- Add a small helper module terraform-module-snapshotter that:
  - calls a lifecycle pre-hook to snapshot DB and object storage prior to apply,
  - records snapshot manifest into state as a read-only output for incident correlation.
- Provider pin snippet to add in repo root versions.tf:
  - terraform {
    required_providers = {
      aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "~> 4.60" }
    }
  }
- Add an acceptance test that runs `terraform plan` against a forked state with simulated partial resources (CI harness) to catch unknown destructive diffs.

Common gotchas (field notes):
- CI applied provider upgrade in same PR as infra changes; the provider change caused resource schema drift. Always separate provider bumps.
- Missing DDB lock removal after abort; leaves terraform locked. Include lock-abort playbook in runbooks.
- WAL retention insufficient for long-running restores. Ensure retention > expected restore window + buffer.

Communication template (incident lead send to customer):
"We’ve paused the live upgrade and captured verified snapshots. We are running a controlled resume/restore operation and estimate service restoration in [X hours]. We will update every 30 minutes and pre-share verification artifacts as the cutover progresses."

Appendix: quick reference commands and scripts
- Check snapshot checksum: sha256sum manifest.json
- Force unlock TF: terraform force-unlock -force <LOCK_ID>
- Import resource: terraform import <address> <id>
- Test KMS decrypt: aws kms decrypt --ciphertext-blob fileb://blob.bin --key-id alias/restore-test --output text --query Plaintext | base64 --decode > plain.bin

Open action items (for engineering):
- (Asha) Draft CI case for provider partial-apply simulation.
- (Diego) Implement terraform-module-snapshotter prototype.
- (Katherine) Add recovery smoke tests to customer acceptance suites.

Notes to reviewers:
This is intentionally pragmatic and contains escape hatches that require explicit approvals (manual state edit, key rewrapping). Please annotate any place where field ops needs a safer alternative or automation.

End of document.
